news.content_title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) News, Articles and Research
news.content: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody that provides season-long protection against RSV in infants, reducing medically attended infections and hospitalizations. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab together offer complementary strategies to protect newborns during their highest-risk months. Overview Feature Articles Latest Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) News and Research Early-infancy infection with RSV increases the risk of developing childhood asthma Belgian scientists from VIB and Ghent University (UGent), together with Danish collaborators, have uncovered compelling evidence that early-infancy infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) significantly increases the risk of developing childhood asthma-especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. Year-round access to RSV immunization may reduce major seasonal outbreaks Providing year-round access to RSV immunization would minimize the risk of large seasonal outbreaks across the nation, including in both urban and rural areas. Preparing for the respiratory virus season: A guide for families As respiratory virus season begins, pediatric experts are preparing for an expected rise in cases of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which can cause cold-like symptoms in most people but serious illness in infants and older adults. COVID-19, RSV, and flu vaccines remain safe and effective The systematic review provides crucial insights into the efficacy and safety of respiratory virus vaccines, supporting evidence-based immunization practices. Study reveals impact of viral combinations on infant respiratory illness severity A new study led by researchers at National Jewish Health has revealed that, while a wide range of viruses can cause lower respiratory tract illnesses (LRIs) in infants, certain viruses and viral combinations dramatically increase the risk of severe disease. A parent's guide to manage pediatric respiratory illnesses during the virus season As we head deeper into fall and toward the holiday season, your little one may start to exhibit symptoms like a runny nose, cough, or fever. HEPA purifiers do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure In a secondary analysis of a study of 200 classrooms, Mass General Brigham researchers found respiratory viral exposures were still high in those with HEPA purifiers, suggesting additional interventions are needed. RSV vaccines protect two most-at-risk groups from severe illness The review demonstrates that vaccines for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are both safe and effective in protecting groups who are most at risk for serious illness, including older adults and infants. Soap shortages undermine global hand hygiene efforts A lack of soap is the most often reported barrier to effective hand hygiene-key to curbing the spread of infection-in shared community spaces, such as households, schools, and public places, finds a systematic review of the available research, published in the open access journal BMJ Global Health. RSV vaccine slashes hospitalizations in older adults in real-world trial A large, real-world randomized trial in Denmark found that the RSVpreF vaccine reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in adults aged 60 and over by over 80%. The vaccine also showed protection against broader respiratory illness with a favorable safety profile. Healthy newborns also face high risk of severe RSV infection It is not only premature babies and children with underlying diseases who suffer from serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections. Can an allergy spray help prevent COVID-19? Researchers determine the efficacy and safety of azelastine nasal spray for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthy adults. How effective is the RSV vaccine for older adults? A single dose of the RSV vaccine offers 58% protection against hospitalization in older adults, but effectiveness varies in immunocompromised individuals. New guidelines improve care for respiratory infections in leukemia patients People with leukemia have a weakened immune system due to the disease itself and treatment, which leads to an increased susceptibility to infections. RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications in older adults Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a well-known cause of infections in children, but it's understudied in older individuals. Maternal RSV vaccination linked to sharp drop in infant lung infections Vaccination of pregnant women has been linked to a drop in newborns being admitted to hospital with a serious lung infection, research suggests. Light-activated drug discovery identifies broad-spectrum antivirals UC Santa Barbara researchers and collaborators from campus biotech spinoff Integrated Biosciences, as well as Harvard, MIT and genomics company Illumina Ventures are using optogenetics - the use of light to probe the functions of living tissue - to find compounds to help our bodies more effectively help themselves in times of physiological stress. How underreporting masks the real impact of RSV in older populations Research shows RSV leads to high hospitalization rates in adults, emphasizing the importance of enhanced surveillance and diagnostic measures in healthcare. New RSV guideline aims to standardize pediatric care across China Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRTIs) in children under five and poses a persistent threat to child health worldwide. WHO releases first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against RSV Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) published its first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – the leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children globally

analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: RSV 导致成人住院率较高,丹麦的一项大型真实世界随机试验发现,RSVpreF 疫苗 将 60 岁及以上成人与 RSV 相关的住院率降低了 80% 以上。单剂量的 RSV 疫苗 可以为老年人提供 58% 的住院保护,但对于免疫功能低下的个体来说,效果有所不同。全年接种 RSV 疫苗可能会减少全国主要季节性 暴发 的发生。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 儿科专家正在为呼吸道病毒季节期间 RSV 病例的预期增加做好准备。孕产妇 疫苗接种 和 尼塞韦单抗 共同提供补充策略,在新生儿风险最高的月份提供保护。世界卫生组织 (WHO) 发布了第一份关于保护婴儿免受 RSV 感染的免疫产品的立场文件。然而,HEPA 净化器并不能完全减少教室病毒暴露,这表明需要采取额外的干预措施。

news.content: News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event SUBSCRIBE Menu SUBSCRIBE Show Search News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event Search Query Submit Search Press Releases U.S. FDA Accepts sBLA for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to Update its Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Lower Respiratory Tract Disease Indication to Include Children Under Two Years at Increased Risk for Severe RSV for Their Second Season August 6, 2026 | 8 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print EMA also accepts application for the same population for ENFLONSIA based on results from the Phase 3 SMART trial If approved, children under two years of age at increased risk for severe RSV disease will be eligible to receive an additional dose of ENFLONSIA for their second RSV season RAHWAY, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--$MRK #MRK--Merck (NYSE: MRK), known as MSD outside of the United States and Canada, announced today that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted a supplemental Biologics License Application (sBLA) for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to expand its indication to include prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) in children under two years of age at increased risk for severe RSV disease through their second RSV season. The FDA has set a Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA), or target action, date of March 22, 2027. In July 2026, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) accepted the application to expand marketing authorization for ENFLONSIA in the European Union (EU) for the same population. ENFLONSIA was approved by the U.S. FDA in June 2025 and by the European Commission in April 2026 for the prevention of RSV LRTD in infants born during or entering their first RSV season. ENFLONSIA is the first and only preventive option against RSV LRTD administered to infants without the need for weight-based dosing. “For some children, the potentially serious impact of RSV does not stop after their first RSV season,” said Dr. Macaya Douoguih, vice president, Therapeutic Area Head, Global Clinical Development, Merck Research Laboratories. “The recent FDA and EMA regulatory filings represent important opportunities to help expand protection with ENFLONSIA for vulnerable children under two years of age during their second RSV season – potentially further reducing the significant burden of RSV on families and health care systems.” Even with protection during their first RSV season, certain children – including those born with chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease or early or moderate preterm birth with certain risk conditions – remain vulnerable to severe RSV disease during their second RSV season. Both the U.S. and EU applications are supported by data from the Phase 3 SMART trial (MK-1654-007), which were presented at RSVVW’26, the 9th conference of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Foundation (ReSViNET), in February 2026 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2025 (interim RSV season 1 results) and JAMA Pediatrics in July 2026 (full results). ENFLONSIA is approved in more than 40 countries worldwide, including the United States, Canada, the European Union, China and Japan, for use in infants during their first RSV season. Regulatory filings are underway for approval in additional countries globally, as well as for indication expansion where already approved. About the Phase 3 SMART Trial The SMART trial (MK-1654-007) (NCT04938830) was a Phase 3, randomized, partially-blind, palivizumab-controlled, multicenter study to evaluate the safety, efficacy and pharmacokinetics of ENFLONSIA in infants and children at increased risk for severe RSV disease over two RSV seasons. The trial enrolled early (<29 weeks gestational age [GA]) or moderate preterm infants (≥29 to ≤35 weeks GA) and infants with chronic lung disease (CLD) of prematurity or congenital heart disease (CHD) of any GA. In RSV season 1, participants were randomized 1:1 to receive either a 105 mg dose of ENFLONSIA (n=502) or monthly palivizumab (n=501) by intramuscular (IM) injection. In RSV season 2, eligible participants (children under 2 years of age with CLD, CHD or early or moderate preterm birth with certain risk conditions) received an additional open-label 210 mg dose of ENFLONSIA by IM injection (n=276, of whom 138 received ENFLONSIA and 138 received palivizumab in RSV season 1). Nearly all participants (99%) who received ENFLONSIA in RSV season 2 had CLD (n=229) or CHD (n=43). About RSV Globally Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a contagious virus that causes widespread seasonal infections and can lead to serious respiratory conditions such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia. As a leading cause of hospitalization among infants globally, there is persisting unmet need for RSV preventive options for both healthy and high-risk infants during their first RSV season as well as for children at increased risk for severe RSV disease through their second RSV season. RSV season is the time of year when RSV infections are most common, usually occurring autumn through spring of the next year in temperate climates. Timing and severity in a given community or region can vary year to year. About ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) in the U.S. ENFLONSIA is Merck’s FDA-approved extended half-life monoclonal antibody (mAb) indicated for passive immunization for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract disease in newborns and infants who are born during or entering their first RSV season. ENFLONSIA is administered using the same dose regardless of weight (105 mg/0.7 mL in a prefilled syringe) and is designed to provide direct, rapid and durable protection through 5 months, a typical RSV season. For infants born during the RSV season, ENFLONSIA is to be administered within the first week of life. For infants born outside of the RSV season, ENFLONSIA should be administered shortly before the RSV season begins. For infants undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass during or entering their first RSV season, an additional 105 mg dose is recommended as soon as the infant is stable after surgery. ENFLONSIA has a 30-month shelf life. Selected Safety Information for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) in the U.S. Do not administer ENFLONSIA to infants with a history of serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, to any component of ENFLONSIA. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been observed with other human immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) monoclonal antibodies. If signs or symptoms of a clinically significant hypersensitivity reaction or anaphylaxis occur, initiate appropriate medications and/or supportive therapy. ENFLONSIA may interfere with some immunologically-based RSV diagnostic assays (i.e., rapid antigen tests) as observed in laboratory studies. Confirmation using a reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay is recommended when rapid antigen assay results are negative and clinical observations are consistent with RSV infection. The most common adverse reactions were injection-site erythema (3.8%), injection-site swelling (2.7%) and rash (2.3%). The FDA has set a Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA), or target action, date of March 22, 2027. In July 2026, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) accepted the application to expand marketing authorization for ENFLONSIA in the European Union (EU) for the same population. ENFLONSIA was approved by the U.S. FDA in June 2025 and by the European Commission in April 2026 for the prevention of RSV LRTD in infants born during or entering their first RSV season. ENFLONSIA is the first and only preventive option against RSV LRTD administered to infants without the need for weight-based dosing. “For some children, the potentially serious impact of RSV does not stop after their first RSV season,” said Dr. Macaya Douoguih, vice president, Therapeutic Area Head, Global Clinical Development, Merck Research Laboratories. “The recent FDA and EMA regulatory filings represent important opportunities to help expand protection with ENFLONSIA for vulnerable children under two years of age during their second RSV season – potentially further reducing the significant burden of RSV on families and health care systems.” Even with protection during their first RSV season, certain children – including those born with chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease or early or moderate preterm birth with certain risk conditions – remain vulnerable to severe RSV disease during their second RSV season. Both the U.S. and EU applications are supported by data from the Phase 3 SMART trial (MK-1654-007), which were presented at RSVVW’26, the 9th conference of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Foundation (ReSViNET), in February 2026 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2025 (interim RSV season 1 results) and JAMA Pediatrics in July 2026 (full results). ENFLONSIA is approved in more than 40 countries worldwide, including the United States, Canada, the European Union, China and Japan, for use in infants during their first RSV season. Regulatory filings are underway for approval in additional countries globally, as well as for indication expansion where already approved. About the Phase 3 SMART Trial The SMART trial (MK-1654-007) (NCT04938830) was a Phase 3, randomized, partially-blind, palivizumab-controlled, multicenter study to evaluate the safety, efficacy and pharmacokinetics of ENFLONSIA in infants and children at increased risk for severe RSV disease over two RSV seasons. The trial enrolled early (<29 weeks gestational age [GA]) or moderate preterm infants (≥29 to ≤35 weeks GA) and infants with chronic lung disease (CLD) of prematurity or congenital heart disease (CHD) of any GA. In RSV season 1, participants were randomized 1:1 to receive either a 105 mg dose of ENFLONSIA (n=502) or monthly palivizumab (n=501) by intramuscular (IM) injection. In RSV season 2, eligible participants (children under 2 years of age with CLD, CHD or early or moderate preterm birth with certain risk conditions) received an additional open-label 210 mg dose of ENFLONSIA by IM injection (n=276, of whom 138 received ENFLONSIA and 138 received palivizumab in RSV season 1). Nearly all participants (99%) who received ENFLONSIA in RSV season 2 had CLD (n=229) or CHD (n=43). About RSV Globally Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a contagious virus that causes widespread seasonal infections and can lead to serious respiratory conditions such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia. As a leading cause of hospitalization among infants globally, there is persisting unmet need for RSV preventive options for both healthy and high-risk infants during their first RSV season as well as for children at increased risk for severe RSV disease through their second RSV season. RSV season is the time of year when RSV infections are most common, usually occurring autumn through spring of the next year in temperate climates. Timing and severity in a given community or region can vary year to year. About ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) in the U.S. ENFLONSIA is Merck’s FDA-approved extended half-life monoclonal antibody (mAb) indicated for passive immunization for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract disease in newborns and infants who are born during or entering their first RSV season. ENFLONSIA is administered using the same dose regardless of weight (105 mg/0.7 mL in a prefilled syringe) and is designed to provide direct, rapid and durable protection through 5 months, a typical RSV season. For infants born during the RSV season, ENFLONSIA is to be administered within the first week of life. For infants born outside of the RSV season, ENFLONSIA should be administered shortly before the RSV season begins. For infants undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass during or entering their first RSV season, an additional 105 mg dose is recommended as soon as the infant is stable after surgery. ENFLONSIA has a 30-month shelf life. Selected Safety Information for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) in the U.S. Do not administer ENFLONSIA to infants with a history of serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, to any component of ENFLONSIA. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been observed with other human immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) monoclonal antibodies. If signs or symptoms of a clinically significant hypersensitivity reaction or anaphylaxis occur, initiate appropriate medications and/or supportive therapy. ENFLONSIA may interfere with some immunologically-based RSV diagnostic assays (i.e., rapid antigen tests) as observed in laboratory studies. Confirmation using a reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay is recommended when rapid antigen assay results are negative and clinical observations are consistent with RSV infection. The most common adverse reactions were injection-site erythema (3.8%), injection-site swelling (2.7%) and rash (2.3%). news.excerpt: As respiratory virus season approaches, doctors recommend that parents consult with pediatricians about new vaccination options to protect infants from RSV.

news.content_title: Rsv season approaches as doctors urge infant protection
news.content: SHREVEPORT, La. ( KTAL/KMSS ) — Fall is quickly approaching, which means respiratory virus season is right around the corner. Doctors say infants are the most susceptible to respiratory viruses. RSV, or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, is the most common virus that puts newborns at risk for pneumonia and airway inflammation. Shreveport doctor urges UV safety during heat rise Experts say the easiest way for parents to protect their little ones is to keep their environment as germ-free as possible. With recent advancements in medicine, physicians say it is best to talk with your child's medical provider to see if vaccinations are best for them. "So, for the first time, families have access to multiple ways to actually build a shield around their newborn before the RSV actually reaches that baby," says Dr. David Janese, family medicine physician with Ochsner LSU Health. PCOS now PMOS: New name reflects broader health impact "So make sure that you stay informed, you're asking questions, you're doing your own research, because when it comes down to it, you're the parent. You're the protector of your child. You have to do what you want to do, and we want to do what's best for the baby," Janese says. Dr. Janese says if your baby has a fever, trouble breathing, and is less responsive, contact your child's pediatrician. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. analysis.brief_en: As fall approaches, U.S. physicians are urging heightened protection for infants against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), the leading cause of pneumonia and airway inflammation in newborns. Dr. David Janese, a family medicine physician with Ochsner LSU Health in Shreveport, Louisiana, highlights new preventive options, including vaccinations, and advises parents to consult their child’s pediatrician. Experts emphasize keeping infants’ environments germ-free and seeking immediate medical attention if symptoms such as fever, breathing difficulties, or lethargy arise. While RSV season looms, no specific case counts or outbreaks are detailed in the guidance, which focuses on proactive measures to shield the most vulnerable.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, August 11, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Nirsevimab Immunization Outcomes in the First Two Years by Bioengineer August 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody designed to protect infants from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), was associated with a substantial reduction in hospitalizations caused by RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections during the first year after administration, according to a study published in JAMA Pediatrics. The findings were observed across both the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons, providing early real-world evidence that the preventive treatment can reduce severe disease requiring hospital care in young children. RSV is one of the most common causes of lower respiratory tract infection in infants and young children. Although infection often produces cold-like symptoms, the virus can spread into the small airways and lungs, causing bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Infants, particularly those born prematurely or with underlying medical conditions, are at increased risk of respiratory distress, dehydration, and hospitalization. Because the virus circulates seasonally and can infect children repeatedly throughout life, reducing the severity of a first infection is a major public health objective. Discover more Drugs & Medications Biological Sciences Health Pharmaceuticals & Biotech Nirsevimab works by providing passive immunity rather than stimulating the infant’s immune system to produce its own antibodies. The drug is a laboratory-engineered antibody that binds to the fusion protein on the surface of RSV. This protein is essential for the virus to enter human cells and spread between them. By attaching to a vulnerable region of the fusion protein, nirsevimab can neutralize RSV particles before they establish infection or limit the progression of infection after exposure. Its extended duration of action allows a single administration to provide protection throughout much of an RSV season. The study evaluated outcomes during two consecutive RSV seasons and compared hospitalization patterns among children who received nirsevimab with those who did not. Its principal focus was hospitalization associated with RSV lower respiratory tract infection, a clinically important endpoint because it reflects severe disease rather than infection detected only through outpatient testing. The investigators also examined whether nirsevimab was associated with changes in hospitalizations from non-RSV infections and asthma, conditions that could help indicate whether the observed effect was specifically linked to RSV prevention. Across the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 seasons, children who received nirsevimab experienced substantially fewer hospitalizations related to RSV lower respiratory tract infections during the first year of follow-up. The consistency of the association across both seasons is notable because the timing and intensity of RSV circulation can vary from year to year. Seasonal differences in viral transmission, population immunity, healthcare-seeking behavior, and the prevalence of other respiratory pathogens can all influence hospitalization rates. Observing a similar protective pattern in two successive seasons strengthens the evidence that the reduction was related to nirsevimab rather than to a single unusual epidemic. The researchers did not find evidence that nirsevimab reduced hospitalizations caused by non-RSV infections. This distinction is biologically important. Nirsevimab targets RSV specifically and does not function as a broad antiviral or general immune stimulant. A selective reduction in RSV-related admissions, without a comparable decline in hospitalizations from unrelated infections, supports the interpretation that the treatment’s benefit is pathogen-specific. It also suggests that the results were not simply the consequence of broader differences in healthcare access, general illness prevention, or the likelihood that treated children were hospitalized. The analysis also found no association between nirsevimab and reduced asthma-related hospitalizations. Asthma is influenced by multiple factors, including genetic susceptibility, airway inflammation, environmental exposures, and viral triggers. Severe RSV infection early in life has been linked in some research with later respiratory problems, but a potential long-term relationship cannot be established by observing short-term hospitalization patterns alone. The absence of a detected reduction in asthma admissions indicates that the immediate preventive effect of nirsevimab should not be interpreted as evidence that the antibody prevents asthma or modifies all forms of respiratory disease. Discover more Medical Literature & Resources infection Respiratory Conditions respiratory respiratory disease The apparent benefit was limited to the first year of follow-up. During the second year, the study did not identify a corresponding reduction in RSV-related hospitalizations. Several explanations are possible. The antibody’s protection is designed to last through a defined period rather than indefinitely, and children may encounter RSV after the period of effective antibody coverage has ended. In addition, older children generally face a different risk profile than infants, with more mature airways and immune systems reducing the likelihood of severe disease. Changes in exposure, vaccination or prophylaxis practices, and the underlying circulation of RSV may also contribute to differences between the first and second years. Because the study was observational, the findings demonstrate an association rather than definitive proof of causation. Treatment decisions, underlying health, birth history, healthcare access, and other characteristics may differ between children who receive nirsevimab and those who do not. Researchers use statistical methods to account for measurable differences, but unmeasured factors can remain. Even so, the results complement clinical trial evidence by showing how nirsevimab performed under routine conditions and across more than one RSV season. The findings suggest that targeted antibody protection can meaningfully reduce severe RSV disease in infants during the period when they are most vulnerable, while underscoring that it does not prevent unrelated infections or guarantee protection beyond the first year. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-10; study covers 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons with outcomes assessed during the first two years after administration.
analysis.location_and_population: Infants and young children, particularly those born prematurely or with underlying medical conditions, in settings where RSV circulates seasonally.
analysis.event: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reported that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, was associated with a substantial reduction in hospitalizations due to RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections during the first year after administration.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study observed substantially fewer RSV-related hospitalizations in children who received nirsevimab compared to those who did not during the first year of follow-up across two consecutive RSV seasons. No reduction was observed in hospitalizations from non-RSV infections or asthma, indicating a pathogen-specific effect. The benefit did not extend to the second year.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is observational and demonstrates an association rather than definitive causation. Differences in treatment decisions, underlying health, birth history, healthcare access, and other characteristics may influence results. The protective effect is limited to the first year, and older children face a lower risk profile. Findings complement clinical trial evidence by showing real-world performance across multiple seasons.

analysis.brief_en: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reports that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, significantly reduced hospitalizations from RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections in infants during the first year after administration. The protective effect was consistent across the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons, with substantially fewer admissions among treated children compared to untreated peers. The benefit was specific to RSV and did not extend to non-RSV infections or asthma-related hospitalizations. Protection waned by the second year, aligning with the antibody’s designed duration of action. Researchers emphasize that while the findings support real-world effectiveness, the study’s observational design limits causal inference and unmeasured factors may influence outcomes.

analysis_en.location_and_population: Infants and young children, particularly those born prematurely or with underlying medical conditions, in settings where RSV circulates seasonally.
analysis_en.event: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reported that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, was associated with a substantial reduction in hospitalizations due to RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections during the first year after administration.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The study observed substantially fewer RSV-related hospitalizations in children who received nirsevimab compared to those who did not during the first year of follow-up across two consecutive RSV seasons. news.source_body_en: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reports that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, significantly reduced hospitalizations from RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections in infants during the first year after administration. The protective effect was consistent across the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons, with substantially fewer admissions among treated children compared to untreated peers. The benefit was specific to RSV and did not extend to non-RSV infections or asthma-related hospitalizations. Protection waned by the second year, aligning with the antibody’s designed duration of action. Researchers emphasize that while the findings support real-world effectiveness, the study’s observational design limits causal inference and unmeasured factors may influence outcomes.

Q&A: Which Hospitalized Children With RTIs Face the Highest Severe Disease Risk? By Lorraine L. Janeczko, MPH - Last Updated: August 7, 2026 Maria Deza Leon, MD More than one in five children hospitalized with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs) develop severe disease, and children transferred from a referring hospital face the highest risk, according to a retrospective study conducted at two Canadian pediatric centers. “In this cohort study of hospitalized children with acute RTIs, many developed severe illness requiring intensive interventions. Chronic conditions were associated with increased risk, whereas viral coinfections were common but not associated with disease severity,” lead author Haifa Mtaweh, MD, PhD, of The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, Ontario, and her coauthors wrote in JAMA Network Open. “Despite low mortality, the complication burden remained high, underscoring the need for targeted prevention and ongoing surveillance.” Risk Factors for Severe Disease The 2,585 enrolled children (median age, 2.5 years) were hospitalized with acute RTIs between July 2022 and June 2023 at The Hospital for Sick Children and BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, British Columbia. Roughly half (50.6%) had at least one chronic condition, with neurologic, developmental, or genetic diagnoses most common. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and enterovirus-rhinovirus were the predominant pathogens identified, at 30.4% and 25.6%, respectively. Severe illness, including cardiac arrest, the need for noninvasive or invasive ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), or kidney replacement therapy, occurred among 551 children (21.3%), and of these, 37 (6.7%) died. In multivariable analysis, children transferred from a referring hospital (adjusted risk ratio [aRR], 4.73; 95% CI, 4.01-5.59), children with a single identified virus compared with none (aRR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.30-2.08), children with two or more chronic conditions compared with none (aRR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.36-1.93), and patients aged less than 1 year and more than 10 years were at increased risk for severe outcomes. Viral coinfections, detected among approximately 15% of patients, were not associated with severity. An Expert Shares Insights Maria Deza Leon, MD, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Children’s Mercy in Kansas City, Missouri, who was not involved in the study, spoke with Physician’s Weekly about the study and its implications for pediatric acute RTI care. Physician’s Weekly: Which complications should clinicians anticipate among children hospitalized with RTIs, and do these risks vary by viral pathogen? Dr. Deza Leon: Common severe complications included acute respiratory distress syndrome, cardiac complications, septic shock, pneumothorax, and empyema, with some children requiring ECMO or kidney replacement therapy. Although complication rates were generally similar across viruses, influenza was more often associated with ARDS and septic shock, whereas human metapneumovirus was more often associated with cardiac complications and extracorporeal support. These findings suggest that viral identification may help inform risk, but clinical management should remain focused on the patient’s overall trajectory. Which chronic conditions place patients at the highest risk for severe outcomes, and how can clinicians use this information to guide individualized care strategies? Children with neurologic, developmental, and genetic disorders carried the greatest risk for severe disease, with chronic pulmonary and cardiac conditions also associated with increased risk. Risk was highest among children with multiple chronic conditions, highlighting the impact of medical complexity on patient outcomes. Clinicians can use this information to identify high-risk patients early and guide management decisions. Children with complex medical conditions may benefit from closer monitoring, a lower threshold for escalation of care, and careful discharge planning. These findings also support prioritizing preventive measures, including routine immunizations, RSV prevention strategies when appropriate, and timely access to specialty care for medically complex children. What factors might explain why the highest risk concentrates in two groups—infants and older children/adolescents? This elevated risk among infants is not unexpected. Smaller airways, reduced physiologic reserve, and immature immune function make young children especially vulnerable to respiratory infections. The increased risk observed among older children and adolescents is particularly noteworthy. Although hospitalization for respiratory tract infections is less common in these age groups than in infancy, those requiring admission may represent a more medically complex population with underlying comorbidities or more severe illness at presentation. These findings suggest that while the overall burden of respiratory disease is highest in infancy, the potential severity of respiratory tract infections in hospitalized adolescents should not be overlooked. How does coinfection influence disease course and outcomes for these patients? One of the more reassuring findings was that viral coinfection did not appear to increase the risk of severe disease. Coinfections were relatively common, occurring in about 15% of cases, but their frequency was similar among children with severe and nonsevere illness. These findings suggest that detecting multiple respiratory viruses should not automatically be considered a predictor of worse outcomes. The study also highlights the challenges of interpreting highly sensitive molecular testing, which can detect residual viral nucleic acid that may not reflect active infection or meaningfully contribute to disease severity. What key insights does this study offer about identifying high‐risk patients, anticipating complications, and optimizing early supportive care? This study serves as an important reminder that severe respiratory infection remains a significant source of pediatric morbidity, even in the post-pandemic era. More than one in five hospitalized children met criteria for severe disease, and nearly one-quarter required pediatric ICU admission. The findings reinforce the importance of focusing on patient-specific risk factors rather than the viral diagnosis alone, with particular attention to children with medical complexity and multiple chronic conditions. Transfer from an outside hospital may also serve as a useful marker of greater illness severity. In addition, the results support continued use of preventive strategies, including vaccination and respiratory syncytial virus-targeted prevention when indicated. Clinicians should also remain alert for nonrespiratory complications, such as cardiac dysfunction and septic shock, particularly in children whose clinical status is worsening. Overall, although mortality was uncommon, the burden of severe illness, intensive care utilization, and associated complications remained substantial, underscoring the importance of early recognition, close monitoring, and aggressive supportive care. Experts recommend closer monitoring and earlier escalation for high-risk patients, alongside routine immunizations and RSV-targeted prevention where indicated.

elements_en.location_and_population: Two Canadian pediatric centers: The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, Ontario) and BC Children’s Hospital (Vancouver, British Columbia); 2,585 hospitalized children with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs), median age 2.5 years.
elements_en.event: Retrospective cohort study reporting that more than one in five hospitalized children developed severe disease; highest risk observed in children transferred from a referring hospital, those with multiple chronic conditions, infants under 1 year, and adolescents over 10 years. Findings published in JAMA Network Open and discussed by an external expert.
elements_en.scale_impact_and_risk: 2,585 enrolled children; 551 (21.3%) met severe illness criteria including cardiac arrest, need for noninvasive or invasive ventilation, ECMO, or kidney replacement therapy; 37 (6.7% of severe cases) died. Chronic conditions (especially neurologic, developmental, or genetic) and transfer status were associated with increased risk; viral coinfections (≈15%) were not associated with severity.
elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Study authors recommend targeted prevention, ongoing surveillance, and prioritizing RSV prevention strategies for medically complex children. Findings emphasize patient-specific risk factors over viral diagnosis alone and highlight challenges in interpreting highly sensitive molecular tests. No active public-health response actions are described in the report.

elements_zh.location_and_population: 两个加拿大儿科中心:病童医院(安大略省多伦多)和 BC 儿童医院(不列颠哥伦比亚省温哥华);2,585 名因急性呼吸道感染 (RTI) 住院的儿童,中位年龄 2.5 岁。
elements_zh.event: 队列研究 回顾性研究报告称,超过五分之一的住院儿童患有严重疾病;从转诊医院转院的儿童、患有多种慢性病的儿童、1 岁以下的婴儿和 10 岁以上的青少年中观察到的风险最高。研究结果发表在《JAMA Network Open》上,并由外部专家进行了讨论。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 2,585名入学儿童;551 名(21.3%)符合严重疾病标准,包括心脏骤停、需要无创或有创通气、ECMO 或肾脏替代治疗;37人(重症病例的6.7%)死亡。慢性疾病(尤其是神经系统疾病、发育疾病或遗传疾病)和转移状态与风险增加相关;病毒合并感染(约 15%)与严重程度无关。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 研究作者建议针对病情复杂的儿童进行有针对性的预防、持续的 监测 以及优先考虑 RSV 预防策略。研究结果强调了患者特定的危险因素而不是单独的病毒 诊断,并强调了解释高度敏感的分子测试的挑战。报告中没有描述积极的公共卫生应对行动。

news.title_zh: 问答:哪些患有 RTI 的住院儿童患严重疾病的风险最高? - 医师周刊
news.source_body_en: A retrospective cohort study of 2,585 Canadian children hospitalized with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs) between July 2022 and June 2023 found that more than one in five developed severe disease, with 21.3% requiring intensive interventions and 6.7% of severe cases ending in death. Risk was highest among infants under one year, adolescents over ten years, children transferred from another hospital, and those with multiple chronic conditions—particularly neurologic, developmental, or genetic disorders. Respiratory syncytial virus and enterovirus-rhinovirus were the most commonly detected pathogens, but viral coinfections did not increase severity. Experts recommend closer monitoring and earlier escalation for high-risk patients, alongside routine immunizations and RSV-targeted prevention where indicated.
news.content_zh: 队列研究 对 2022 年 7 月至 2023 年 6 月期间因急性呼吸道感染 (RTI) 住院的 2,585 名加拿大儿童进行的回顾性研究发现,超过五分之一的儿童出现严重疾病,其中 21.3% 需要强化干预,6.7% 的严重病例最终死亡。一岁以下的婴儿、十岁以上的青少年、从另一家医院转院的儿童以及患有多种慢性病(尤其是神经系统、发育或遗传疾病)的患者的风险最高。呼吸道合胞病毒 和肠道病毒-鼻病毒是最常检测到的病原体,但病毒合并感染并没有增加严重程度。专家建议对高危患者进行更密切的监测并尽早升级,并在有需要时进行常规免疫和针对 RSV 的预防。

supplementary_news.content: SHREVEPORT, La. ( KTAL/KMSS ) — Fall is quickly approaching, which means respiratory virus season is right around the corner. Doctors say infants are the most susceptible to respiratory viruses. RSV, or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, is the most common virus that puts newborns at risk for pneumonia and airway inflammation. Shreveport doctor urges UV safety during heat rise Experts say the easiest way for parents to protect their little ones is to keep their environment as germ-free as possible. With recent advancements in medicine, physicians say it is best to talk with your child's medical provider to see if vaccinations are best for them. "So, for the first time, families have access to multiple ways to actually build a shield around their newborn before the RSV actually reaches that baby," says Dr. David Janese, family medicine physician with Ochsner LSU Health. PCOS now PMOS: New name reflects broader health impact "So make sure that you stay informed, you're asking questions, you're doing your own research, because when it comes down to it, you're the parent. You're the protector of your child. You have to do what you want to do, and we want to do what's best for the baby," Janese says. Dr. Janese says if your baby has a fever, trouble breathing, and is less responsive, contact your child's pediatrician. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved.
